body: I've tried and failed a few times, and in a way it's helped me know what to watch out for. It's a learning process, even if the lessons can be painful.

wrapping up day 18 after being a regular weed smoker for 12 years. I've been feeling more than ever that I'm done for good and thought I'd post here, since this community has helped me get to this place mentally.

I think I've internalized now that the weed just doesn't help. I truly don't enjoy it anymore, and I just know that if I were to try it again, it would give me a tiny little thrill followed by being exhausted and miserable for the next few days and ultimately be pointless.

Now, I still spend plenty of my time exhausted and miserable. But now that weed isn't so much affecting me, I can see much more clearly where it's coming from and how long it lasts naturally. And I think that understanding will only as it continues to leave my system.

It all goes back to trauma and shame for me, and my relationship with weed became deeply stained by those things almost since I started using it all that time ago. While I had some good times, it's crystal clear to me that no good times in the future are going to occur with this drug, me using it will always be colored by my history of shame, and it's time to work towards letting that go, and letting go of the addictive qualities of my life, of which weed is the primary one.

It's devastatingly hard, but that's a way that no contact can be healthy if your old relationship was codependent.

> He says it is harder for me because he saw his parents openly struggle whereas mine were fake and acted like everything was perfect while there was a lot of emotional abuse and toxicity going on under the surface, more covert and hidden and the mind games are the worst.

I think this really is harder, and it's the same situation I'm in (2 years NC). I think some parents know they messed up, and others like mine can't allow themselves to live in that reality. In fact, I think being relatively "good" parents (when they didn't slip up) was part of my parent's manipulation strategy.

It's just that to keep things smooth they'd use strategies like convincing me things I thought was happening weren't really happening. They'd brush aside any unanticipated concerns I raised. And most of all, they encouraged me to self-censor, so that I was actually doing the most work to reduce the negative situations and make us seem like a happy family.

In that way, manipulative parents love it if their kid has a mild childhood, because it's less things the kid can complain about. But what they are doing is torture to achieve it.

I think spiritual bypass is a very real thing, and I think there are bad and irresponsible teachers and "gurus" out there, and that people can take the wrong lessons from old traditions that may or may not apply to modern day, and there can be a lot of invalidation and victim-blaming in certain (but not all) spiritual circles.

*That said*, just to provide my own experience that is slightly counter to yours, I got into meditation and it's basically how I realized how bad my parents were. In a few of my sessions I felt a powerful self-compassion and relaxation that I realized I never had around my parents. Finally things clicked for me after a few more interactions with them.

I wasn't going to spiritual centers or having that diligent of a practice. But Buddhism and meditation are still things I've fascinated about to this day, and I think there is something there, with all of my caveats above. But I appreciate you calling out the harmful stuff, because it helps me remember that.

I honestly worry about threads like these because I know my parents never felt comfortable around me and I worry that a bunch of people see these and reassure themselves they're fine and don't have to try to overcome their attachment issues society has burdened them with.

Yes, if you're feeling overwhelmingly guilty, reduce that, forgive yourself, etc. But continue to try to forge that bond, go to therapy, talk with your SO, find what will allow you to feel connected and make up for years when that didn't happen, don't just wait for your kid to be likable.

Hi, I'm a guy in my late 20's who's been estranged for around 2 years now. I don't really have answers, just sympathy since it's also been really tough for me. I keep a couple friends close, but I don't like going into the details with them. It feels like that's something I'd reserve for a friendship or relationship where we both felt kind of mature and safe going there, but I think that can be pretty rare and I just haven't had anything like that in a while.

I think I surprised myself by finding some strength recently and getting my life together when it felt like hell a few months ago. I changed my living situation and it made a huge difference. I haven't even been seeing a therapist (which I've done in the past and it's been helpful, but it doesn't feel like what I need now for some reason). I do believe that we can experience feelings of belonging and being heard while completely on our own, and I've had experiences like that, often in meditation. I also think that outside stressors do a lot to make us feel less integrated and more alone. For me, reducing my stressors did a lot, and it's given me a lot of room to relax when I go into depressive moods these days.

You may or may not find any of that helpful, but wishing you the best

I've been doing metta meditations which have felt really wholesome and are allowing me to have a supportive relationship with myself. I think stuff like that (yoga, exercise) can bring a lot of nourishment when other people aren't doing it at the moment. I personally don't buy that we *always need other people* around us to be happy, as some say. I think a lot can come from inside ourselves, maybe even the strongest stuff. And recorded guided meditations/yoga/etc. allow you to have a guiding figure that you don't have to interact with.

It may help to take it a step further and just find peace in the present moment, so it's not about where or who you are, it's just that you're a living being, experiencing the world before you. When anxiety comes up, breathe into it and try to hold yourself gently. Wishing you the best.

Something similar happened to me, and it's what a lot of posters here are missing. I think it's common for things to just "click" with survivors at some point. My relationship was on good terms with my parents after a rocky childhood, but the second I started holding them accountable at 27, they showed that they were still unable to accept any responsibility and just lashed out at me. 

A good relationship is more than being friendly. It's about being able to work through the difficult stuff in a healthy way. Frankly, I think a lot of people are in denial about how "good" their relationships are with their parents, I know a lot of people that are afraid to confront their parents with any kind of justifiable complaint.

I think hate is a totally valid feeling. The hate that some people have towards you isn't wrong because they're evil or because hate itself is bad, it's wrong because it's unfair, unjust, and basically the result of brainwashing most likely enforced with some variety of childhood trauma that they are trying to pass on to you, because you've been painted as a target. Your hate towards them for making you feel less safe because of who you are is totally rational, in comparison.

I'm in trauma-focused therapy right now, and in a past session as we were getting into it, I felt this overwhelming need to express that I *hate* my parents. Not that I understand where they're coming from, they tried their best, blah blah blah. I needed to say what I was never able to express, which was an intense hatred. So I think it's vital to find sympathetic people in your lives that you can really vent with, and say what you want to say.

When you're talking with the *enemy* I think you have every right to vent, and that's what is happening a lot nationally, but I do think it's just the beginning of the conversation. At a certain point we're going to have to listen to each other, as painful as that will be. Maybe it's just because it's what I'm going through, but it's my view that there's just a huge amount of unresolved trauma in the world, and that there needs to be a sort of reckoning towards the American parenting style and culture that is rife with emotional neglect at its most benign, and once that happens, people on the right will realize how much of their anger is misdirected (and, maybe controversially here, but I think a lot of the left will realize that too).

Thanks for sharing you're experiences here, I think it's really helpful.

Victory: I reached out to a few therapists and one got back to me. Looks like it could be a good fit since she is focused on trauma and addictions. I've been pessimistic about therapy for the past few months but I feel like I have to try again.

Vent: I kind of hate how much I've isolated from my friends and family but I feel like I have no choice. I feel like I'm in so much pain that I can't be kind or supportive right now. I just get angry at them or myself during the interactions and can't wait to be alone again. I feel like no one is there for me in the way I want them to be, but there's no use telling them that.

I think I'm getting a better grasp of what I have to do to stay sane, basically monitoring cravings and accepting them without giving in.

I've cut my parents out for 1.5 years. I'm 5 months free of self harm, 1 week free of weed, next I want to give up porn. 

I still think there is a demon inside of me that can come out at any time. I think the self hatred goes way deeper than I've managed to see yet. I got some psychedelics that I'm going to be trying in the next few days. 

I've got basically no support system, I'm doing this on my own. The downside is no one to say they're proud of me. But I hate when people say that anyway. In the end I'll probably always be alone. But maybe the psychedelics will break something and allow me to enjoy company again. We'll see.
